display_value:
Notre Dame Learning and the broader Notre Dame community of faculty and staff focused on teaching and learning need fundamental, baseline information about faculty and their levels of knowledge, use, and comfort with generative AI technology in their teaching. This collaborative project team from the Lab for AI in Teaching and Learning will conduct a university-wide needs assessment that will inform the university’s support services and resources for faculty in this critical area. The results of this focused survey will be particularly important in informing the activities of ND Learning but the information will be widely shared and presented for other colleagues at the university to use in informing their own activities e.g., OIT, library, Provost.

This project will be led by faculty and staff in the Lab for AI in Teaching and Learning. Kevin R. Guidry will serve as the primary project manager with significant and ongoing collaboration with the lab’s director, Alex Ambrose, and Vice President and Associate Provost for Teaching and Learning Ron Metoyer. We are also collaborating with IRIS to administer this University-wide faculty survey.

Proposed project timeline:

* July 2025: Project intake, initial planning, Submit IRIS survey request form, first survey draft
* August 2025: Liaise with IRIS, finalize survey
* September 2025: Deploy survey in second week of September
* October 2025: Close survey and analyze results
* November 2025: Share preliminary results
* December 2025 and January 2026: Write report
* February 2026: Share results with ND community

display_value:
Hello Kaneb Center Staff,

My name is Chloe Jones, I am a 4th year PhD candidate in physics and also act as our department's graduate student outreach committee chair. I wanted to connect with you on a potential collaboration opportunity this summer for teaching certification for graduate students in our program. 

This summer, the physics graduate student organization's outreach committee will be hosting the second annual installment of PING@ND (Physicists Inspiring the Next Generation). PING is a program originally hosted at MSU, which has since expanded to our department as of last year. PING is a two-week summer program, happening this year from July 6th - 17th, where local high school students through the TRIO / Upward Bound program are invited and supported while getting hands-on experiences with physics. Some of our endeavors, under graduate student instruction and guidance, involve (a) learning how to plan and execute an experiment, (b) analyzing data through boosting their coding skills, (c) learning about the college experience and how to apply to college if they so desire, and (d) practicing their professional development and presentation skills through a final presentation. The hope is that PING gives students interested in physics the unique opportunity to learn more about what it means to be a physicist.

Since this program is graduate-student planned and led, from the logistical standpoint all the way through the daily instruction and lesson planning, we are hoping to give interested GS instructors further incentive to help with the program. Our thought was to institute a possible teaching certification or other teaching requirement that could be met by participating as an instructor. In order to discuss the possibility and logistics of this, I am hoping to meet with a representative from the Kaneb Center soon to discuss this. Would this be something that we can collaborate on? I have also discussed this idea with our department's Director of Graduate Studies, Anna Simon-Robertson, who has agreed to help facilitate this from the faculty's standpoint if required.

Let me know if this is a feasible plan, and if so when/where we can meet to discuss. Thank you for your time!

display_value:
CHEM 10172 ("Orgo I") and BIO 10172 (Molecules to Ecosystems, "M2E") both run in the Spring semester and have an overlap of students enrolled in them. Both courses are using versions of assessment wrappers. The literature indicates that completing more wrappers in different, but simultaneous, courses ("dosage") leads to greater benefits. We would like to investigate if that holds true for the students in CHEM/BIO 10172. Additionally, because the wrapper implementations are different, it could be possible that students who participate in only one implementation might lead to more positive outcomes than students who participate only in the other implementation. In short, there are many things to look at and we are seeking assistance in deciding on concrete research questions and methods to measure them and then the resources we need to do so.

This project scopes and supports a collaboration between the University of Notre Dame and Google to produce a public-facing video case study highlighting the use of Gemini and NotebookLM tools in learning, teaching, and institutional work at Notre Dame.
Google will lead all filming, editing, and post-production and will publish the resulting media as part of its higher education marketing efforts. ND Learning / LAITL will serve as the primary institutional coordinator, supporting participant identification, messaging alignment, internal approvals, and on-campus logistics.
The project will result in:
One long-form video (~2 minutes) featuring Notre Dame leaders, faculty, and students


Three to four short-form social videos (~1 minute each) featuring additional faculty and students


Potential joint marketing and PR distribution across Google and Notre Dame channels


This initiative advances Notre Dame’s strategic goals related to AI literacy, responsible AI adoption, and national leadership in teaching and learning with AI, while requiring careful coordination due to its external visibility, brand implications, and legal approvals.

A codebook of common themes and detailed categorization of ideas with representative quotes

A report with in-depth analysis and a proposed AI framework to be shared with summit participants and the ND community

A presentation summarizing the results and recommendations for Provost/Dean/DUS leadership 

Post AI Summit NDL Communications web article or news story

A conference poster presentation of the results

[Converted to project] Evaluating Generative AI as a Critical Thinking Tutor in God and the Good Life
display_value:
This study evaluates the effectiveness of a generative AI tutor, co-developed by Paul Blaschko and Roberto Casarez, in supporting undergraduate students’ development of critical thinking skills through argument mapping in God and the Good Life. The AI tutor will be deployed on a custom chatbot platform integrated into Thinker Analytix, using a prompt designed and iteratively tested by Paul and Roberto to align with course pedagogy.
Throughout the semester, students will engage with the AI tutor to receive feedback, clarify philosophical concepts, and revise their arguments. The research will assess the quality and impact of these interactions and compare learning outcomes between students supported by AI and TAs versus traditional TA-only support. Evaluation methods include pre-course, mid-course, and post-course assessments, interaction analysis, and perception surveys from students and TAs. The goal is to better understand how AI can enhance instruction in the humanities and support scalable, high-impact teaching models.

Maximizing Mendoza is a two-part course for first-year and transfer business students, each part is one credit: Maximizing Mendoza I, offered in the Fall Semester and focused on academic discernment, and Maximizing Mendoza II, offered in the Spring Semester and focused on career discernment. Currently optional, the goal is to create sufficient capacity so that every first-year business student can take both courses. While Mendoza undergraduates consistently achieve high employment rates upon graduation, the college's undergraduate career outcomes metrics lag behind those of peer institutions that also rank in the top 10 of national rankings of undergraduate business programs. This disparity arises because first- and second-year students have limited engagement with career development, receive insufficient preparation for internship recruitment, and lack a formal discernment process. We’d like to create a two-course sequence in which the classes are thematically and meaningfully connected, ultimately creating a signature experience for Mendoza students.

Maximizing Mendoza I (MMI) has been offered for the past three years with growing popularity. In Fall 2025, 189 students were enrolled across two sections of the course. In Fall 2026, we believe there could be demand for as many as three or four sections, accommodating 300 to 400 Mendoza first-year and transfer students. It aims to ensure that all business students are welcomed to the college and begin to develop a positive sense of belonging, while also setting the high expectations that being a part of the Mendoza community entails. It showcases a survey of the academic offerings provided by each of the college’s five academic departments, availability of various campus resources, and a framework for students to assess their personal values and use those to evaluate options and make key decisions.

Maximizing Mendoza II (MMII) is completing its pilot in Spring 2026, with the aim of providing insights into career pathways and industry trends. This is because the Meruelo Family Center for Career Development focuses on securing internships and jobs and does not support students in discernment or career readiness. Students will also learn the importance of their professional brand and the most effective way to build their own in a positive, intentional manner. 14 students are enrolled this semester, and their feedback has been positive. We would like to begin scaling this second section to eventually be available to more first-year and transfer students, potentially 200 to 300 in Spring 2027 and in subsequent years, as many or more than those who enroll in Maximizing Mendoza I.

display_value:
This is a request that ODL is putting in on behalf of Ming Hu.

Project Summary
A persistent challenge in engineering education is the limited attention paid to communication skills— particularly when engineering students must convey sustainability-related ideas to non-technical audiences. While students are taught to analyze data and solve technical problems, they are rarely trained to articulate these insights clearly in writing, through visualizations, or in conversation. This project addresses that gap by embedding structured communication training within an interdisciplinary sustainability curriculum. The approach is grounded in the Engineering for One Planet (EOP) framework and is supported by strong institutional infrastructure, including Notre Dame’s Sustainability and Real Estate Minors.

Objectives
1. Embed communication-intensive assignments into sustainability-focused engineering courses, using case studies on carbon-neutral design, life cycle thinking, and circular economy.
2. Train students in multimodal communication strategies—including technical writing, data storytelling, stakeholder mapping, and systems diagramming—to enhance their ability to explain complex systems to both expert and public audiences.
3. Evaluate communication outcomes using rubrics, peer reviews, and pre/post assessments across multiple dimensions: clarity, persuasiveness, visual effectiveness, and audience awareness.

Educational Approach
Rather than adding separate communication courses, the project integrates communication practice directly into core coursework. For example, students will simulate design charrettes, prepare
sustainability reports, and present policy briefs as part of existing assignments. Communication instruction will be co-designed with faculty in engineering, architecture, and business, and supported by
Notre Dame’s Teaching and Learning Center.

Anticipated Outcomes
• Improved student capacity to communicate complex sustainability topics through writing, speech, and visual media
• Reusable communication modules and rubrics for integration into STEM courses
• Enhanced preparation of students for interdisciplinary collaboration and public-facing roles

Additional notes from Discovery Meeting with Ming:
- The pilot will start with Ming's course first and then be expanded
- She would like this to run in the Fall 2026
- Ming has availability in the Spring and plenty of availability in the summer
- Ming has funding for 2 undergraduate students as well as funding for materials & supplies (VR headsets) and consultant costs

display_value:
I run a Fellows program for Notre Dame undergrads interested in anti-poverty research. We hire about 20+ undergraduate research interns each summer and pair them with research faculty or research associates in labs across campus. Right now, all of the students use Stata to varying extents in their roles. They're cleaning datasets, coding, analyzing data and creating visualizations, etc. 

For the last two summers, two of the full-time pre-doctoral research associates at LEO (one of the labs where we place interns) developed and taught a "Stata bootcamp" to all of the interns in the first two weeks of their summer internship. The bootcamp is a 16-hour in-person course that starts with the basics and gradually introduces students to various functionalities of Stata. They're using real data, as opposed to mostly "clean" datasets that students see in their econometrics classes.

We're interested in taking this curriculum and turning it into a course for the Fellows in the program. Maybe online modules, or recorded videos + exercises, and maybe the research associates offer "office hours" but don't need to physically teach the course each summer. This is where we could use your expertise and help to imagine what's possible.

In the coming years, we expect the program to grow and we'd love to be able to offer this not only to the ND undergrads who are interns, but also new pre-doctoral research associates who don't often receive in-depth Stata training in their undergraduate courses.

In collaboration with the JTS Initiative (Arun) and Undergraduate Education (Fr. Dan), we are working on a course for Notre Dame students that will take place at the Borgo (Castel Gondolfo - the Pope's Summer Residence) on the intersection of sustainability and faith—a living lab of the encyclical, Laudato Si. The five day long course intended to be taking by ND students and eventually students from Universities across the world, have five 8 hour days of instruction, each with a central theme. We are seeking to tape 4, 8-10 videos by experts that will be a part of each day's focus on that topic. Day 1: The theological and environmental connections of sustainability (Arun and Fr. Dan will do this one); Day 2: Water quality, pollution, etc.; Day 3: Alternative energy sources; Day 4: Circular food production and waste.

We are approaching ND professors to give these short content talks. We are piloting the course with 8 ND students over spring break and then a full class of 20 students will take the course in May after graduation. We would like to have the videos in time for the pilot in March, with the hopes of having videos completed by the middle of February.

display_value: The 4-year NSF project aims to establish a scalable and sustainable training platform for workforce development in data chemistry. The platform, named C2D (Cybertraining for Chemical Data scientists), integrates adaptive learning and assessment with personalized recommendations for training materials regarding the application of machine learning in synthetic chemistry, thereby enabling personalized instruction in the field of data chemistry. Starting from a survey and focus groups analysis involving domain experts, the C2D will develop a blueprint for curating curricular material that is fed into a personalized recommender system based on continuous adaptive assessment. It organizes training videos, reading, implementation codes and assessments in a way that is responsive to the needs of the learners and will be offered to the academic, industrial, and general population free of charge. The C2D works with a number of academic and industrial partners to ensure the wide adoption and sustainability of the platforms. In the short term, this project aims to train 300-500 data chemists, including students, postdocs, and established professionals in academia and industry, through collaboration with the 14 member institutions and >10 industrial partners of C-CAS (the NSF Center for Computer Assisted Synthesis) who indicated a strong interest in training in data chemistry. We have published an open-access tutorial book: https://data-chemist-handbook.github.io/. The next step (in year 3) is to build a self-paced learning system based on this tutorial book.

display_value:
We would love to have support designing and implementing a new course in the Sheedy Business Explorers Program. This program, which launches next year, will be a year-long, application-based program for first-years in the College of Arts and Letters who are discerning whether to pursue a career in business.

Incoming first year students will be recruited before arriving at Notre Dame. Accepted students will be enrolled in a 3 credit course to be taken over an entire academic year called “Business for Humans” focused on developing a broader understanding of core areas of business (e.g. finance, consulting, management).

In addition, they will attend talks with visiting Sheedy speakers, and will be encouraged to sign up for select Sheedy events (e.g. workshops, office hours with visiting speakers).

Successful participants in this program will be recruited to apply for the Sheedy Family Program in the spring of the following year.

We envision piloting this program with 40 students, and demand suggests that, with the appropriate resources, we could meet an expected demand of 80-100 students per year at full capacity.

We envision the course having some distinctive elements that help students understand the broad sweep of a life/career and the ways an Arts & Letters major can add value to it. This might include producing videos with representative alumni or perhaps custom designing a game that students play throughout the course.

I'd like to ask for assistance from the Office of Digital Learning in developing an app for students in the Department of Music and the Graduate Program in Sacred Music.

The project involves leveraging ND's Gemini subscription to create a tool that generates high-quality translations and IPA transcriptions for foreign language song lyrics. This would be a significant improvement over many of the resources currently available to our students. In the future, the app might also include text-to-speech recordings of these texts at variable speeds.

The app would ensure that all students get the same high-quality output, regardless of their familiarity with AI prompts. Gemini has already helped me create a model, but I need some help to make it fully-functional.

display_value:
I run a Fellows program for Notre Dame undergrads interested in anti-poverty research. We hire about 20+ undergraduate research interns each summer and pair them with research faculty or research associates in labs across campus. Right now, all of the students use Stata to varying extents in their roles. They're cleaning datasets, coding, analyzing data and creating visualizations, etc. 

For the last two summers, two of the full-time pre-doctoral research associates at LEO (one of the labs where we place interns) developed and taught a "Stata bootcamp" to all of the interns in the first two weeks of their summer internship. The bootcamp is a 16-hour in-person course that starts with the basics and gradually introduces students to various functionalities of Stata. They're using real data, as opposed to mostly "clean" datasets that students see in their econometrics classes.

We're interested in taking this curriculum and turning it into a course for the Fellows in the program. Maybe online modules, or recorded videos + exercises, and maybe the research associates offer "office hours" but don't need to physically teach the course each summer. This is where we could use your expertise and help to imagine what's possible.

In the coming years, we expect the program to grow and we'd love to be able to offer this not only to the ND undergrads who are interns, but also new pre-doctoral research associates who don't often receive in-depth Stata training in their undergraduate courses.

display_value:
Notre Dame Learning and the broader Notre Dame community of faculty and staff focused on teaching and learning need fundamental, baseline information about faculty and their levels of knowledge, use, and comfort with generative AI technology in their teaching. This collaborative project team from the Lab for AI in Teaching and Learning will conduct a university-wide needs assessment that will inform the university’s support services and resources for faculty in this critical area. The results of this focused survey will be particularly important in informing the activities of ND Learning but the information will be widely shared and presented for other colleagues at the university to use in informing their own activities e.g., OIT, library, Provost.

This project will be led by faculty and staff in the Lab for AI in Teaching and Learning. Kevin R. Guidry will serve as the primary project manager with significant and ongoing collaboration with the lab’s director, Alex Ambrose, and Vice President and Associate Provost for Teaching and Learning Ron Metoyer. We are also collaborating with IRIS to administer this University-wide faculty survey.

Proposed project timeline:

* July 2025: Project intake, initial planning, Submit IRIS survey request form, first survey draft
* August 2025: Liaise with IRIS, finalize survey
* September 2025: Deploy survey in second week of September
* October 2025: Close survey and analyze results
* November 2025: Share preliminary results
* December 2025 and January 2026: Write report
* February 2026: Share results with ND community

Comparing assessment wrapper dose effects on student performance in simultaneous courses
display_value:
CHEM 10172 ("Orgo I") and BIO 10172 (Molecules to Ecosystems, "M2E") both run in the Spring semester and have an overlap of students enrolled in them. Both courses are using versions of assessment wrappers. The literature indicates that completing more wrappers in different, but simultaneous, courses ("dosage") leads to greater benefits. We would like to investigate if that holds true for the students in CHEM/BIO 10172. Additionally, because the wrapper implementations are different, it could be possible that students who participate in only one implementation might lead to more positive outcomes than students who participate only in the other implementation. In short, there are many things to look at and we are seeking assistance in deciding on concrete research questions and methods to measure them and then the resources we need to do so.

[Converted to project] Evaluating Generative AI as a Critical Thinking Tutor in God and the Good Life
display_value:
This study evaluates the effectiveness of a generative AI tutor, co-developed by Paul Blaschko and Roberto Casarez, in supporting undergraduate students’ development of critical thinking skills through argument mapping in God and the Good Life. The AI tutor will be deployed on a custom chatbot platform integrated into Thinker Analytix, using a prompt designed and iteratively tested by Paul and Roberto to align with course pedagogy.
Throughout the semester, students will engage with the AI tutor to receive feedback, clarify philosophical concepts, and revise their arguments. The research will assess the quality and impact of these interactions and compare learning outcomes between students supported by AI and TAs versus traditional TA-only support. Evaluation methods include pre-course, mid-course, and post-course assessments, interaction analysis, and perception surveys from students and TAs. The goal is to better understand how AI can enhance instruction in the humanities and support scalable, high-impact teaching models.
